Via Egnatia
VEE-uh eg-NAH-shuh
noun (proper name; place)
Latin via (road) + Egnatia (after the proconsul Gnaeus Egnatius who built it); the Roman highway across the Balkans by which Paul carried the gospel into Europe.

Biblical Definition

The Via Egnatia was the great Roman road that ran from the Adriatic coast across Macedonia and Thrace to Byzantium, the eastern continuation of the Appian Way and one of the chief highways of the empire — and along its course the apostle Paul carried the gospel into Europe. When Paul crossed from Asia into Macedonia after the vision of the man who cried "Come over and help us" (Acts 16:9), he landed at Neapolis and went up to Philippi, a city on the Via Egnatia, where Lydia was converted and the Philippian jailer was saved. The road then bore him westward to Amphipolis and Apollonia and to Thessalonica, and on toward Berea — the very cities to which his later epistles would be written. The Roman peace and the Roman roads, built for legions and trade, became in God's providence the arteries of the gospel; the empire that would persecute the church first paved the way for her message. This dictionary marks the Via Egnatia as a witness to that providence: the Lord of history ordered the roads of Caesar so that the good news of Christ might run swiftly from city to city, and the kingdoms of men served, all unknowing, the spread of the kingdom of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

The great Roman highway across Macedonia and Thrace by which Paul carried the gospel into Europe — linking Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea. A witness that God ordered the roads and peace of Caesar's empire for the swift spread of the good news of Christ.

VIA EGNATIA, proper noun. The Roman highway from the Adriatic across Macedonia and Thrace to Byzantium.

The eastern continuation of the Appian Way, one of the chief roads of the empire.

Linked Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica — cities of Paul's mission.

Paul carried the gospel into Europe along its course after the Macedonian vision (Acts 16:9).

A witness that God ordered Caesar's roads for the spread of the gospel.

Key Scripture

Acts 16:9 — "And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us."

Acts 17:1 — "Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where was a synagogue of the Jews."

Gal 4:4 — "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."

Rom 10:15 — "how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no real redefinition; the danger is only a thin secular reading that sees in Paul's use of the Roman roads mere historical accident or clever strategy, and misses the providence of God who ordered the highways of empire for the running of His gospel.

expand to see more

The only corruption that threatens the Via Egnatia is the flattening of providence into accident. The secular historian sees a missionary who shrewdly used the imperial road network; and Paul did use it. But Scripture sees more: that when the fulness of time was come, God sent forth His Son (Gal 4:4), and that same God had prepared the stage — a common Greek tongue, a Roman peace, and Roman roads like the Via Egnatia — so that the gospel might run. The kingdoms of men served the kingdom of God all unaware.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God over history. Paul did not stumble into Europe; he was called by a vision (Acts 16:9) and carried by a road Rome had built for other ends. How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace (Rom 10:15) — and how wonderful that God paved the road beneath those feet. The Via Egnatia preaches that the Lord of history bends the works of empires to the errand of His Son.
